newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam says no decision reached on devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam says no decision reached on devaluation.

text.p: The State Bank of Vietnam said in a statement on Tuesday that no decision had been reached on whether to devalue the local currency, the dong.

Apparently rowing back on a report in the semi-official weekly Vietnam Investment Review, the central bank said that when Governor Cao Si Kiem mentioned the possibility of devaluation he was citing expert opinion rather than making a policy statement.
"The State Bank of Vietnam's governor has not issued any directives or announcement in written form regarding the exchange rate in the coming months," it said.

"Recently, at some meetings, the State Bank of Vietnam's governor quoted opinions of some experts outside the banking field on...exchange rate management, including a suggestion that the dong be devalued by the State Bank of Vietnam," the statement said.
"The governor's purpose is to let the bank's consultancy bodies study the suggestion as a reference in the process of working out monetary policy," it added.
It said the central bank was continuing to manage the exchange rate according to supply and demand, and with the aim of monetary stability and speeding up economic growth.

Kiem was quoted in the Vietnam Investment Review's September 23 edition as saying "interest rates will be cut further and exchange rates will be raised in the coming months" to ensure high economic growth and tackle the country's trade deficit.
Sources at the central bank who declined to be named said that "raising interest rates" meant raising the number of dong per foreign currency unit, which would amount to a devaluation.
The dong has been steady at around 11,000 per dollar for several years.

Bankers and economists say a cut in the value of the dong could help trim the trade gap, which stood at a record $3.25 billion in the first eight months of this year -- a near-sixfold increase from the same period of 1995.
